title: Dedicated capacity graceful-degradation corridors and tenant flow-control PRD
creator: Sofia Alvarez
description:
Problem: During transient capacity pressure and cross-tenant contention, Dedicated customers experience unpredictable failures or large latency spikes. Existing mechanisms (hard preemption, emergency eviction, and simple burst windows) are either too blunt or too risky for customers with strict throughput needs. We need a production-grade, predictable graceful-degradation system that gives tenants explicit, auditable knobs to trade latency, throughput, and cost when capacity is constrained.

This PRD proposes the concept of 'Degradation Corridors' paired with 'Tenant Flow-Control' — a set of executable policies, telemetry, and UI/CLI controls that allow Redwood and customers to: 1) define ordered degradation paths for each tenant, 2) control per-tenant request shaping and concurrency ceilings, 3) select safe spillover targets (lower-cost model variants, lower-priority pools, or burst accelerator capacity), and 4) orchestrate automated, reversible scale-downs with clear rollout and rollback rules.
problem_statement: Unpredictable failures and opaque preemption during high contention in Dedicated pools create customer churn risk and operational toil. Customers want: deterministic degradation, configurable fallbacks, predictable cost behavior under pressure, and auditability of decisions made by the platform.
goals: Offer per-tenant degradation policies that preserve availability and provide predictable latency trade-offs under constrained capacity
Provide flow-control primitives (concurrency ceilings, adaptive slowdown, token buckets) exposed via API and Console
Enable automated spillover to defined fallback targets (compatible model variants, opportunistic burst lanes, or downgraded quantization profiles) with safety checks
Make all decisions auditable, reversible, and observable in Console and telemetry
Minimize unintended customer outages and reduce oncall interventions during contention events
non_goals: Replace dedicated reservation semantics — reservations still guarantee baseline capacity; Degradation Corridors apply when reservations cannot be honored
Implement new low-level GPU scheduling kernels — this project leverages existing runtime primitives exposed by ENG teams
Guarantee zero-latency impact in all cases — the feature's intent is controlled trade-offs, not magic preservation of original SLOs
requirements: Policy model: JSON-based per-tenant policy that lists ordered degradation steps (e.g., reduce concurrency -> enable prefix caching -> switch to quantized variant -> route to opportunistic pool)
Flow-control primitives: API for configuring concurrency_limit, burst_tokens, and adaptive_slowdown parameters per-tenant
Fallback targets: Ability to register fallback model variants and target pools with compatibility labels and bounded latency/cost profiles
Safeguards: Minimum health checks before promotion of a fallback; must not increase observed error-rate beyond customer-configured threshold
Observability: Console UI showing active corridor, current step, triggered reasons, p95/p99 latency deltas, error-rate, and weekly audit log of corridor activations
Rollback: Automated rollback conditions (e.g., sustained errors > 2% for 5m) and manual one-click rollback from Console
API parity: All Console controls must be available through Redwood API/SDKs for infra automation
Integration: Play nicely with Dedicated autoscaling and reserved pool hot-standby features — corridor activations should not permanently consume reserved capacity buckets
Permissions: RBAC such that only org-admins or assigned operators can edit corridors and approve escalations
Telemetry: Emit structured events for corridor changes and per-tenant degradation_step events to existing telemetry streams (metrics + trace tags)
acceptance_criteria: A tenant policy can be created via API and Console that contains at least three ordered degradation steps

In a controlled canary (internal test tenant), when we trigger a simulated capacity shortfall, the platform advances through the corridor steps in order and emits the expected structured telemetry events

When a fallback to a quantized model variant occurs, output correctness regressions are measured against baseline on provided eval set and remain within customer-configured tolerances (default 1.5% quality delta)
Console shows real-time corridor state, including the current step, time entered, triggered metrics, and the operator who made manual overrides
Automated rollback is exercised in a canary: intentionally trigger a rollback condition (error rate > threshold) and verify the system reverses the last step and logs the action
No new critical production incidents (P0) attributable to corridor logic during a 30-day staged rollout to select Dedicated customers
API and Console access respects RBAC and audit logs contain the actor, time, and changed fields for all policy edits
success_metrics: Reduce P99 burst-induced evictions by >= 65% for participating Dedicated tenants within 60 days of rollout
Reduce oncall paging for dedicated capacity contention by >= 40% for impacted services
90% of corridor activations are automated (not manual) after 6 weeks in opt-in cohorts
Customer-reported availability complaints for Dedicated plans fall by 50% in pilot cohort
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (2 wks): Design review and API schema finalization with ENG + Security
Phase 1 (4 wks): Implement policy model, telemetry events, and basic Console UI; internal dogfooding with infra teams
Phase 2 (2 wks): Canary with 3 willing Dedicated customers (opt-in) with close monitoring and rollback capability
Phase 3 (4 wks): Gradual ramp to 20 customers, iterate on defaults and UI clarity based on feedback
Phase 4: Full availability in dedicated-2026.04 with documentation, runbook, and post-rollout retrospective
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Misconfigured corridors could degrade customer outputs unexpectedly. Mitigation: Require eval-set validation step for any fallback that changes model variant; provide safe default policies and warnings in Console.
Risk: Corridor logic may interact poorly with autoscaler and cause oscillation. Mitigation: Add hysteresis windows and a coordination handshake with autoscaler (ENG-4312).
Risk: Complex policy surfaces increase support load. Mitigation: Ship curated presets (conservative, balanced, aggressive) and provide one-click rollback and read-only previews for support agents.
Risk: Security/privilege escalation via API. Mitigation: Enforce RBAC checks and require two-step approval for policy application to production tenants; security review required.
Risk: Observability blind spots. Mitigation: Emit structured events and instrument end-to-end traces for corridor activations (ENG-4920).
open_questions: What default degradation presets are acceptable to legal/compliance for regulated customers?
Should corridor activations be billable events (e.g., if spillover uses different cost profiles)? How do we show cost delta to customer in Console?
How aggressively should the platform attempt automated remediation versus notifying operators? Default is automated for conservative presets but we need product guidance.
How to represent multi-tenant group policies for customers with multiple org teams (org-level override vs project-level policy)?
notes: Design sketch: Console will have a visual timeline showing corridor steps and live metric overlays (latency, error-rate, token-per-second). Link to mock: https://drive.redwood.example/mock-corridor-2026
We should coordinate with Pricing for how cost changes are surfaced and whether spillover to opportunistic pools consumes customer credits differently
Follow-up: plan a tooling RFC that details autoscaler handshake; tag ENG-4312 owner (Nina Roberts) for coordination
